analysis.one_liner: Requires brand-name and generic drug companies to disclose settlement deals to antitrust enforcers.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with a bipartisan group of seven senators, was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in April 2003 and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a brand-name drug company and a would-be generic competitor settle a patent fight, the settlement can include payments to the generic maker to delay launching a cheaper copy — so patients keep paying brand-name prices. This bill would have required both companies to file such agreements with the Justice Department and the Federal Trade Commission within ten business days, giving antitrust enforcers timely notice so they could police deals that restrain competition. Companies that failed to file could face fines of up to $11,000 per day.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who buy prescription drugs, especially seniors and families paying out of pocket, because faster scrutiny of brand-generic deals could speed the arrival of cheaper generic drugs. Taxpayers and insurers also benefit from lower drug spending. Antitrust enforcers gain an early-warning system they currently lack.

how_it_helps.text: The bill's stated purpose is to enhance competition for prescription drugs by strengthening the ability of the Justice Department and the FTC to enforce existing antitrust laws regarding brand-name and generic drugs [S3].

It requires any brand-name drug company and generic drug applicant that strike a deal about manufacturing, marketing, sale, or the 180-day generic exclusivity period to file the agreement's text with the Justice Department's Antitrust Division and the FTC within ten business days [S2][S3].
It backs the requirement with a civil penalty of up to $11,000 per day of noncompliance, recoverable by the United States or the FTC, plus court orders compelling compliance [S2][S3].

Congress' own findings in the bill state that deals between patent-holding brand companies and generic makers could restrain trade, reduce competition, and increase prescription drug costs for Americans, and that enhancing competition can significantly reduce those costs [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug companies and generic drug applicants bear new filing and compliance costs, and the brand industry loses some of the secrecy that has let it buy off generic challenges. If enforcement succeeds in unwinding delay deals, drug manufacturers forgo settlement payments and extended monopoly profits.

drawbacks.text: Mandatory disclosure could chill legitimate settlements. Not every brand-generic deal is anticompetitive — some simply resolve a patent fight early and set a certain date for generic entry, which can serve consumers. Filing every such agreement with antitrust enforcers, backed by daily fines, raises the cost and risk of settling at all, which could push more cases into lengthy litigation [S3].

The bill adds a new compliance regime for drug companies, with filings, deadlines, and penalty exposure of up to $11,000 per day, and it charges the FTC with writing implementing rules — administrative costs that are real even if modest relative to drug spending [S2][S3].

Disclosure alone does not ban any deal; it only notifies enforcers, who must still build antitrust cases under existing law. Critics could fairly say the bill creates paperwork without directly outlawing the payments that delay generic competition [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is potentially large and broadly shared: earlier scrutiny of the deals that keep cheaper generics off the market, in a market where generic entry typically slashes prices. The costs — compliance paperwork and some chilled settlements — are real but modest, and the bill takes care to exempt ordinary supply, equipment, employment, and packaging contracts from filing [S3]. The main design weakness is that it is a transparency tool, not a prohibition: it arms enforcers rather than stopping pay-for-delay outright. On balance, a reasonable, low-cost measure aimed at lowering drug prices.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced the bill in April 2003 and sent it to the Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Senator Patrick Leahy introduced the Drug Competition Act of 2003 on April 29, 2003, joined by five Democratic and one Republican cosponsor, including Senator Chuck Grassley [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary [S5].
No further action appears in the record — no hearings, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — and the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, leaving the bill dead in committee [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers came out ahead: the deals they strike with generic challengers remain private and unreviewed at the filing stage, and the extended brand-name sales those deals can produce were untouched. Patients continued paying brand-name prices longer than they would have if such deals faced prompt antitrust review.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsors were bipartisan at introduction — one Republican (Grassley) among seven senators — but it died in a Republican-controlled Judiciary Committee without ever reaching a recorded vote, so no roll call shows where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill forces disclosure of their settlement deals with generic challengers to antitrust enforcers within ten business days, with daily fines for noncompliance. These deals, which can include payments to delay generic entry, are what keep cheaper copies off the market and patients paying brand prices [S2][S3].

Generic applicants must also file any settlement agreement, adding compliance obligations and fines for noncompliance. But the bill targets the deals that delay their market entry, and generic makers as a class gain a clearer path to launching cheaper drugs sooner [S2][S3].
